claim: Neuropathic pain is caused by a lesion or disease of the somatosensory system.
source: Neuropathic pain (NP) is caused by a lesion or disease of the somatosensory system and is characterized by abnormal hypersensitivity to stimuli and nociceptive responses to non-noxious stimuli, affecting approximately 7–10% of the general population.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about neuropathic pain in the abstract.

claim: Neuropathic pain is characterized by abnormal hypersensitivity to stimuli and nociceptive responses to non-noxious stimuli.
source: Neuropathic pain (NP) is caused by a lesion or disease of the somatosensory system and is characterized by abnormal hypersensitivity to stimuli and nociceptive responses to non-noxious stimuli, affecting approximately 7–10% of the general population.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the characteristics of neuropathic pain.

claim: Neuropathic pain affects approximately 7–10% of the general population.
source: Neuropathic pain (NP) is caused by a lesion or disease of the somatosensory system and is characterized by abnormal hypersensitivity to stimuli and nociceptive responses to non-noxious stimuli, affecting approximately 7–10% of the general population.
evidence: This is cited as established knowledge about the prevalence of neuropathic pain.

claim: Current first-line drugs for neuropathic pain like non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents and opioids have limitations including dose-limiting side effects, dependence, and tolerability issues.
source: However, current first-line drugs like non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents and opioids have limitations, including dose-limiting side effects, dependence, and tolerability issues.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about current treatment limitations.

claim: High-frequency terahertz stimulation at approximately 36 THz effectively alleviates neuropathic pain symptoms in mice with spared nerve injury.
source: In this study, we discovered that the high-frequency terahertz stimulation (HFTS) at approximately 36 THz effectively alleviates NP symptoms in mice with spared nerve injury.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The frequency of approximately 36 THz resonates with the carbonyl group in the filter region of Kv1.2 channels.
source: Computational simulation suggests that the frequency resonates with the carbonyl group in the filter region of Kv1.2 channels, facilitating the translocation of potassium ions.
evidence: This is supported by computational simulation data presented in the study.

claim: High-frequency terahertz stimulation facilitates the translocation of potassium ions through Kv1.2 channels.
source: Computational simulation suggests that the frequency resonates with the carbonyl group in the filter region of Kv1.2 channels, facilitating the translocation of potassium ions.
evidence: This is supported by computational simulation data.

claim: High-frequency terahertz stimulation reduces the excitability of pyramidal neurons in the anterior cingulate cortex.
source: In vivo and in vitro results demonstrate that HFTS reduces the excitability of pyramidal neurons in the anterior cingulate cortex likely through enhancing the voltage-gated K+ and also the leak K+ conductance.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo and in vitro experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: High-frequency terahertz stimulation enhances voltage-gated K+ conductance in pyramidal neurons of the anterior cingulate cortex.
source: In vivo and in vitro results demonstrate that HFTS reduces the excitability of pyramidal neurons in the anterior cingulate cortex likely through enhancing the voltage-gated K+ and also the leak K+ conductance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from patch clamp recordings.

claim: High-frequency terahertz stimulation enhances leak K+ conductance in pyramidal neurons of the anterior cingulate cortex.
source: In vivo and in vitro results demonstrate that HFTS reduces the excitability of pyramidal neurons in the anterior cingulate cortex likely through enhancing the voltage-gated K+ and also the leak K+ conductance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from patch clamp recordings.

claim: Neuropathic pain is often a consequence of nerve injury or diseases such as cancer, diabetes mellitus, infection, autoimmune disease, and trauma.
source: NP refers to a debilitating chronic pain condition, which is often a consequence of nerve injury or of the diseases such as cancer, diabetes mellitus, infection, autoimmune disease, and trauma (Baron et al., 2010; Shan et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The symptoms of neuropathic pain include spontaneous pain, hyperalgesia, and mechanical allodynia.
source: The symptoms of NP include spontaneous pain, hyperalgesia, and mechanical allodynia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about neuropathic pain symptoms.

claim: Neuropathic pain is often resistant to currently available drug treatments, including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and even opioids.
source: Unfortunately, NP is often resistant to currently available drug treatments, including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and even opioids (Jensen and Finnerup, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Neuropathic pain is not merely a symptom of a disease but rather an expression of pathological operations of the nervous system.
source: More evidences reveal that NP is not merely a symptom of a disease but rather an expression of pathological operations of the nervous system (Costigan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Optogenetics has demonstrated therapeutic potential in neuropathic pain.
source: Optogenetics, as an interdisciplinary approach, has demonstrated therapeutic potential in NP.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about optogenetics applications.

claim: The limitations of viral vector delivery systems in humans are well-known.
source: However, the limitations of viral vector delivery systems in humans are well-known (Liu and Wang, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A 34.88 THz wave resonates with Aβ protein, disrupting the process of fibril formation.
source: For instance, our previous study demonstrated that a 34.88 THz wave resonates with Aβ protein, disrupting the process of fibril formation (Peng et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous research.

claim: The band of 42.55 THz resonates with the stretching mode of either the –COO- or the –C=O group significantly enhancing the Ca2+ conductance.
source: Li et al. discover that the band of 42.55 THz resonates with the stretching mode of either the –COO- or the –C=O group significantly enhancing the Ca2+ conductance (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: 48.2 THz photons greatly increase the permeability of the sodium channel by a factor of 33.6 through breaking the hydrated hydrogen bonding network between the hydrosphere layer of the ions and the carboxylate groups.
source: Zhu et al. conclude that 48.2 THz photons greatly increase the permeability of the sodium channel by a factor of 33.6 through breaking the hydrated hydrogen bonding network between the hydrosphere layer of the ions and the carboxylate groups (Zhao et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The frequency of 53.5 THz has been reported to enhance the voltage-gated K+ currents, which modulate the startle response and associative learning.
source: Additionally, the frequency of 53.5 THz has been reported to enhance the voltage-gated K+ currents, which modulate the startle response and associative learning (Zhang et al., 2021a; Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The anterior cingulate cortex plays a crucial role in pain regulation.
source: The anterior cingulate cortex plays a crucial role in pain regulation (Bliss et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Nociceptive information resulting from nerve injury is transmitted to the ACC.
source: Our previous research has demonstrated that nociceptive information resulting from nerve injury is transmitted to the ACC (Tsuda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous research.

claim: The ACC exhibits pre- and postsynaptic long-term plasticity, which contributes to chronic pain and associated negative emotions.
source: This region exhibits pre- and postsynaptic long-term plasticity (LTP), which contributes to chronic pain and associated negative emotions (Chen et al., 2014; Koga et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Descending projection pathways from the ACC enhance the neuronal activity of the spinal dorsal horn and regulate nociceptive sensory transmission.
source: Furthermore, descending projection pathways from the ACC enhance the neuronal activity of the spinal dorsal horn (SDH) and regulate nociceptive sensory transmission (Chen et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Brain imaging and MRI studies provide evidence of hyperexcitability in the ACC during both acute and chronic pain.
source: Brain imaging and MRI studies also provide evidence of hyperexcitability in the ACC during both acute and chronic pain (Alles and Smith, 2018; Bliss et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The activity of pyramidal cells in the ACC is directly correlated with the expression of chronic pain.
source: Specifically, the activity of pyramidal cells in the ACC is directly correlated with the expression of chronic pain (Zhu et al., 2022; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Optogenetic excitation of ACC pyramidal cells induces pain.
source: Optogenetic excitation of ACC pyramidal cells induces pain, while their inhibition leads to analgesia (Kang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of ACC pyramidal cells leads to analgesia.
source: Optogenetic excitation of ACC pyramidal cells induces pain, while their inhibition leads to analgesia (Kang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Voltage-dependent potassium (Kv) channels have been proposed as potential target candidates for pain therapy.
source: Neuronal excitability is influenced by various types of voltage-gated ion channels and among them, voltage-dependent potassium (Kv) channels, as one of the important physiological regulators of neuronal membrane potentials, has been proposed as potential target candidates for pain therapy (Takeda et al., 2011; Du and Gamper, 2013; Sakai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Enhancing Kv currents in injured dorsal root ganglion neurons alleviates neuropathic pain.
source: Zhao et al. have reported that enhancing Kv currents in injured dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons alleviates neuropathic pain (Zhao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Lumbar (L)5 spinal nerve ligation (SNL) leads to a time-dependent decrease in Kv1.2-positive neurons in the ipsilateral L5 DRG.
source: Additionally, Fan et al. have demonstrated that lumbar (L)5 spinal nerve ligation (SNL) leads to a time-dependent decrease in Kv1.2-positive neurons in the ipsilateral L5 DRG.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Rescuing Kv1.2 expression in the injured L5 DRG attenuates the development and persistence of pain hypersensitivity.
source: However, rescuing Kv1.2 expression in the injured L5 DRG attenuates the development and persistence of pain hypersensitivity (Fan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A pronounced absorption peak at approximately 36 THz was observed for the potassium channel.
source: Our results revealed a pronounced absorption peak at approximately 36 THz for the potassium channel, which exhibited a considerable board band compared to the absence of a corresponding peak for the sodium channel (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by spectral absorption analysis data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The sodium channel does not show a corresponding absorption peak at approximately 36 THz.
source: Our results revealed a pronounced absorption peak at approximately 36 THz for the potassium channel, which exhibited a considerable board band compared to the absence of a corresponding peak for the sodium channel (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by spectral absorption analysis data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The van der Waals radius of the -C=O groups of the Kv1.2 channel filter structure expanded by approximately 0.5 Å following absorption of THz photons.
source: Our findings indicated a significant kinetic change in the -C=O groups of the channel filter structure, as evidenced by an expansion of its van der Waals radius by approximately 0.5 Å (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: During exposure to THz photons, the conductance of the potassium ion channel exhibited an almost linear increase with the intensity of the THz field.
source: Furthermore, during exposure to THz photons, the conductance of the potassium ion channel exhibited an almost linear increase with the intensity of the THz field, while the conductance of sodium ions remained largely unchanged (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: During exposure to THz photons, the conductance of sodium ions remained largely unchanged.
source: Furthermore, during exposure to THz photons, the conductance of the potassium ion channel exhibited an almost linear increase with the intensity of the THz field, while the conductance of sodium ions remained largely unchanged (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Under terahertz photonic influence, the cortical neurons model showed significantly decreased discharge.
source: Interestingly, under terahertz photonic influence, the cortical neurons model showed significantly decreased in discharge (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The FWHM of action potentials in the THz-exposed group decreased to 95% of the control group.
source: Our observations revealed that the FWHM of action potentials in the THz-exposed group decreased to 95% of the control group (Figure 1f, red column), and the firing frequency experienced a reduction of approximately 70% after THz photon stimulation (Figure 1f, green column).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The firing frequency experienced a reduction of approximately 70% after THz photon stimulation.
source: Our observations revealed that the FWHM of action potentials in the THz-exposed group decreased to 95% of the control group (Figure 1f, red column), and the firing frequency experienced a reduction of approximately 70% after THz photon stimulation (Figure 1f, green column).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: THz photons primarily attenuate neuronal firing activity by increasing potassium ion conductance.
source: These results collectively suggest that THz photons primarily attenuate neuronal firing activity by increasing potassium ion conductance, thereby modulating neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results presented.

claim: HFTS had no significant effect on the activation and inactivation curve slope, half-activation and half-inactivation voltage and time constants (tau) for half-activation and half-inactivation voltage of Nav channels.
source: Upon illumination with ~36 THz photons (0.3±0.05 mW) for durations of 5, 10, and 20 min, we observed that HFTS had no significant effect on the activation and inactivation curve slope, half-activation and half-inactivation voltage and time constants (tau) for half-activation and half-inactivation voltage (Figure 2c–f).
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recording data shown in Figures 2c-f.

claim: HFTS does not affect Nav channel-mediated currents.
source: These findings indicate that HFTS does not affect Nav channel-mediated currents.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on Nav channels.

claim: The application of HFTS induced a significant increase in the amplitude of K+ currents.
source: Our results demonstrated that the application of HFTS induced a significant increase in the amplitude of K+ currents (Supplementary file 1a) and an enhanced slope of the current-voltage characteristic (I-V) curve (Figure 2h–j), without affecting the half-activation voltage (Figure 2k).
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recording data shown in Figures 2h-j and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: HFTS enhanced the slope of the current-voltage characteristic (I-V) curve of K+ currents.
source: Our results demonstrated that the application of HFTS induced a significant increase in the amplitude of K+ currents (Supplementary file 1a) and an enhanced slope of the current-voltage characteristic (I-V) curve (Figure 2h–j), without affecting the half-activation voltage (Figure 2k).
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recording data shown in Figures 2h-j.

claim: HFTS does not affect the half-activation voltage of K+ currents.
source: Our results demonstrated that the application of HFTS induced a significant increase in the amplitude of K+ currents (Supplementary file 1a) and an enhanced slope of the current-voltage characteristic (I-V) curve (Figure 2h–j), without affecting the half-activation voltage (Figure 2k).
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recording data shown in Figure 2k.

claim: The Kv current were enhanced 20 min post-HFTS.
source: It was observed that the Kv current were enhanced 20 min post-HFTS (Figure 2l, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recording data shown in Figure 2l and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: HFTS induced a significant increase of KLeak currents at holding potential at –40 and –30 mV.
source: We found that HFTS also induced a significant increase of KLeak currents at holding potential at –40 and –30 mV (Figure 2n; Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recording data shown in Figure 2n and Supplementary file 1c.

claim: HFTS at approximately 36 THz influences Kv currents and affects KLeak channel activity, resulting in an acceleration of potassium ion flow and an increase in potassium conductance in PYRACC neurons.
source: These experiments demonstrated that HFTS at approximately 36 THz not only influenced Kv currents but also affected KLeak channel activity, resulting in an acceleration of potassium ion flow and an increase in potassium conductance in PYRACC neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on K+ currents.

claim: There was a significant increase in the spike frequency in SNI mice compared to sham mice.
source: Our findings revealed a significant increase in the spike frequency in SNI mice (Figure 3a; Supplementary file 2a), which was effectively rescued by the application of HFTS (Figure 3b) (Supplementary file 2b), but not by 465 nm blue light stimulation (BLS) (Figure 3c; Supplementary file 2c).
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recording data shown in Figure 3a and Supplementary file 2a.

claim: The increased spike frequency in SNI mice was effectively rescued by the application of HFTS.
source: Our findings revealed a significant increase in the spike frequency in SNI mice (Figure 3a; Supplementary file 2a), which was effectively rescued by the application of HFTS (Figure 3b) (Supplementary file 2b), but not by 465 nm blue light stimulation (BLS) (Figure 3c; Supplementary file 2c).
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recording data shown in Figure 3b and Supplementary file 2b.

claim: 465 nm blue light stimulation (BLS) did not rescue the increased spike frequency in SNI mice.
source: Our findings revealed a significant increase in the spike frequency in SNI mice (Figure 3a; Supplementary file 2a), which was effectively rescued by the application of HFTS (Figure 3b) (Supplementary file 2b), but not by 465 nm blue light stimulation (BLS) (Figure 3c; Supplementary file 2c).
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recording data shown in Figure 3c and Supplementary file 2c.

claim: The spike frequency in sham mice decreased after the application of HFTS.
source: Furthermore, the spike frequency in sham mice also decreased after the application of HFTS (Figure 3d) (Supplementary file 2d).
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recording data shown in Figure 3d and Supplementary file 2d.

claim: In SNI mice, there was a decrease in the rheobase compared to sham mice.
source: In SNI mice, we observed a decrease in the rheobase and an elevation in the resting membrane potential (RMP) compared to those in sham mice.
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recording data.

claim: In SNI mice, there was an elevation in the resting membrane potential (RMP) compared to sham mice.
source: In SNI mice, we observed a decrease in the rheobase and an elevation in the resting membrane potential (RMP) compared to those in sham mice.
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recording data.

claim: The alterations in rheobase and RMP in SNI mice were reversed by the application of HFTS.
source: However, these alterations were reversed by the application of HFTS, while BLS had no effects.
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recording data shown in Figures 3g-h.

claim: BLS had no effects on the alterations in rheobase and RMP in SNI mice.
source: However, these alterations were reversed by the application of HFTS, while BLS had no effects.
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recording data.

claim: Voltage threshold, amplitude, and half-width of the action potentials were not different between SNI or sham mice with and without HFTS.
source: Other parameters, such as voltage threshold, amplitude, and half-width of the action potentials, were not different between SNI or sham mice with and without HFTS (Figure 3f–k).
evidence: This is supported by patch clamp recording data shown in Figures 3f-k.

claim: HFTS affects the activity of PYRACC neurons through its specific impact on Kv and KLeak channels.
source: Given that the spike firing, rheobase, and RMP are closely related to low-threshold Kv channels and KLeak channels (Takeda et al., 2011; Tsantoulas and McMahon, 2014; González et al., 2012), these results suggest that HFTS affects the activity of PYRACC neurons through its specific impact on Kv and KLeak channels.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data combined with cited knowledge about ion channels.

claim: There was a significant decrease in the mean firing rate of ACC neurons after HFTS application in both the sham and SNI groups.
source: Our findings revealed a significant decrease in the mean firing rate of ACC neurons after HFTS application in both the sham and SNI groups (Figure 4c and g).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo multi-channel recording data shown in Figures 4c and 4g.

claim: In the sham group, 63.4% of PYRACC neurons exhibited a decrease in firing rate after HFTS.
source: In the sham group, we observed that 63.4% of PYRACC neurons exhibited a decrease in firing rate, 10.8% of PYRACC showed an increase, and 25.8% of PYRACC remained unchanged (93 well-isolated PYRACC neurons were recognized out of 108 total recorded units).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo multi-channel recording data.

claim: In the sham group, 10.8% of PYRACC neurons showed an increase in firing rate after HFTS.
source: In the sham group, we observed that 63.4% of PYRACC neurons exhibited a decrease in firing rate, 10.8% of PYRACC showed an increase, and 25.8% of PYRACC remained unchanged (93 well-isolated PYRACC neurons were recognized out of 108 total recorded units).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo multi-channel recording data.

claim: In the sham group, 25.8% of PYRACC neurons remained unchanged in firing rate after HFTS.
source: In the sham group, we observed that 63.4% of PYRACC neurons exhibited a decrease in firing rate, 10.8% of PYRACC showed an increase, and 25.8% of PYRACC remained unchanged (93 well-isolated PYRACC neurons were recognized out of 108 total recorded units).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo multi-channel recording data.

claim: In the SNI group, 61.8% of PYRACC neurons exhibited decreased activity after HFTS.
source: In the SNI group, we found that 61.8% of PYRACC neurons exhibited decreased activity, 20.3% of PYRACC showed increased activity, and 17.9% of PYRACC remained unchanged (123 well-isolated PYR neurons were recognized out of 130 total recorded units) (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo multi-channel recording data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: In the SNI group, 20.3% of PYRACC neurons showed increased activity after HFTS.
source: In the SNI group, we found that 61.8% of PYRACC neurons exhibited decreased activity, 20.3% of PYRACC showed increased activity, and 17.9% of PYRACC remained unchanged (123 well-isolated PYR neurons were recognized out of 130 total recorded units) (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo multi-channel recording data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: In the SNI group, 17.9% of PYRACC neurons remained unchanged in activity after HFTS.
source: In the SNI group, we found that 61.8% of PYRACC neurons exhibited decreased activity, 20.3% of PYRACC showed increased activity, and 17.9% of PYRACC remained unchanged (123 well-isolated PYR neurons were recognized out of 130 total recorded units) (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo multi-channel recording data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The increased mean firing rate of PYRACC neurons in SNI mice was significantly inhibited by the application of HFTS.
source: Consistently, the increased mean firing rate of PYRACC neurons in SNI mice was significantly inhibited by the application of HFTS (Figure 4h).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo multi-channel recording data shown in Figure 4h.

claim: The activity of INTACC tended to decrease after HFTS.
source: The activity of INTACC also tended to decrease after HFTS (Figure 4i).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo multi-channel recording data shown in Figure 4i.

claim: BLS has no effect on the mean firing rate on the PYRACC and INTACC in both sham and SNI mice.
source: In contrast, BLS has no effect on the mean firing rate on the PYRACC and INTACC in both sham and SNI mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo multi-channel recording data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: HFTS reduces the spike firing of ACC neurons.
source: These results indicate that HFTS reduces the spike firing of ACC neurons, whereas BLS does not have the same effect.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vivo recording data.

claim: BLS does not reduce the spike firing of ACC neurons.
source: These results indicate that HFTS reduces the spike firing of ACC neurons, whereas BLS does not have the same effect.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vivo recording data.

claim: SNI treatment significantly decreased the PWMTs compared to the sham group.
source: We compared the paw withdrawal mechanical thresholds (PWMTs) before and after HFTS (0.3±0.05 mW at the tip of the optic fiber) application for 15 min and found that SNI treatment significantly decreased the PWMTs compared to the sham group.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data.

claim: After the application of HFTS, the PWMTs significantly increased in SNI mice, even surpassing those in the sham group in the first 30 min.
source: However, after the application of HFTS, the PWMTs significantly increased, even surpassing those in the sham group in the first 30 min (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The analgesic effect of HFTS lasted for around 160 min with a 15 min application.
source: The analgesic effect lasted for around 160 min with a 15 min application of HTFS and lasted for around 140 min with a 10 min application of HTFS, suggesting a correlation between the duration of analgesia and the intensity of stimulation (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The analgesic effect of HFTS lasted for around 140 min with a 10 min application.
source: The analgesic effect lasted for around 160 min with a 15 min application of HTFS and lasted for around 140 min with a 10 min application of HTFS, suggesting a correlation between the duration of analgesia and the intensity of stimulation (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: There is a correlation between the duration of analgesia and the intensity of HFTS stimulation.
source: The analgesic effect lasted for around 160 min with a 15 min application of HTFS and lasted for around 140 min with a 10 min application of HTFS, suggesting a correlation between the duration of analgesia and the intensity of stimulation (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral test data.

claim: The PWMTs did not significantly change in the SNI group with the application of 465 nm blue light.
source: In contrast, the PWMTs did not significantly change in the SNI group with the application of 465 nm blue light.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data.

claim: SNI treatment significantly altered the standing time, the stand index, the max contact area, the mean print area, the mean intensity and the duty cycle of the left hind paw.
source: We found that SNI treatment significantly altered the standing time, the stand index, the max contact area, the mean print area, the mean intensity and the duty cycle (Figure 5g–l).
evidence: This is supported by Catwalk gait analysis data shown in Figures 5g-l.

claim: SNI mice tend to avoid standing and walking on their injured hind paw due to pain hyper sensitivity.
source: This suggests that the SNI mice tend to avoid standing and walking on their injured hind paw due to pain hyper sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Catwalk gait analysis data.

claim: The application of HFTS rescued most of the altered gait parameters in SNI mice.
source: The application of HFTS but not BLS rescued most of the above parameters, indicating HFTS' strong analgesic effect.
evidence: This is supported by Catwalk gait analysis data shown in Figures 5g-l.

claim: BLS did not rescue the altered gait parameters in SNI mice.
source: The application of HFTS but not BLS rescued most of the above parameters, indicating HFTS' strong analgesic effect.
evidence: This is supported by Catwalk gait analysis data.

claim: High-frequency terahertz photons alleviate neuropathic pain in the SNI mice by decreasing the excitability of pyramidal neurons in the ACC.
source: In the present study, we provide evidence that high-frequency terahertz photons alleviate neuropathic pain in the SNI mice by decreasing the excitability of pyramidal neurons in the ACC.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The mechanism underlying the effect of HFTS is that it increases voltage-gated potassium ion conductance through resonance with the carbonyl group in the potassium channel filter region.
source: The mechanism underlying this effect is that HFTS increases voltage-gated potassium ion conductance through resonance with the carbonyl group in the potassium channel filter region (Figure 6).
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism based on simulation and experimental data.

claim: Unlike optogenetic technology, HFTS can directly regulate the conformation of the ion channel without delivering a transgene that encodes a light-response protein.
source: Unlike optogenetic technology, HFTS can directly regulate the conformation of the ion channel without delivering a transgene that encodes a light-response protein.
evidence: This is a comparison drawn from the nature of the HFTS technology.

claim: HFTS exhibits frequency selectivity and dependence on channel structure.
source: It exhibits frequency selectivity and dependence on channel structure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: HFTS has the potential to serve as a novel optical technology for the treatment of NP pathology.
source: This research suggests that HFTS has the potential to serve as a novel optical technology for the treatment of NP pathology.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about the potential application of HFTS.

claim: Neuropathic pain is closely associated with nociceptor excitability in the ACC.
source: Neuropathic pain is closely associated with nociceptor excitability in the ACC (Bliss et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2018a; Xu et al., 2008), with ion channels playing a fundamental role in determining neuronal excitability, particularly in the hyperexcitability of pyramidal neurons (Trimmer, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ion channels play a fundamental role in determining neuronal excitability, particularly in the hyperexcitability of pyramidal neurons.
source: Neuropathic pain is closely associated with nociceptor excitability in the ACC (Bliss et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2018a; Xu et al., 2008), with ion channels playing a fundamental role in determining neuronal excitability, particularly in the hyperexcitability of pyramidal neurons (Trimmer, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Nav channel inhibitors are commonly used in neurology as antiepileptic drugs.
source: Excitatory Nav channels, responsible for initiating and depolarizing the action potential, can be targeted by inhibitors to effectively decrease or eliminate electrical excitability. These inhibitors are commonly used in neurology as antiepileptic drugs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Nav channel inhibitors.

claim: Retigabine, an activator for Kv7, has recently been approved as a first-in-class antiepileptic drug.
source: For instance, retigabine, an activator for Kv7, has recently been approved as a first-in-class antiepileptic drug (Gao et al., 2022; Maljevic and Lerche, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Kv1.2 is the most prevalent Kv channel in neuronal membranes.
